items.title: 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal
items.summary: Ukraine's leader had said the deal with Russia to release diesel into the US would help Moscow fund the war.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.
The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.
"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".
Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 the country has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.
Global fuel supplies, including diesel, have been severely limited by the war against Iran launched by the US and Israel, which led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil products usually flows.
Russia - a major producer - and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes on each other's energy infrastructure and transport facilities, further straining energy markets.
"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump continued.
"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."
Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev described Trump's intervention as "iconic and historic", saying that Ukraine "needs leadership actually focused on peace".
The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.
Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.
Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
The Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.
A Downing Street spokesperson said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Zelensky and offered his "complete solidarity".
The pair had agreed Russia should acquiesce to "an immediate energy ceasefire" and end its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea, the spokesperson said, as "this would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market".
News of the US-Russia diesel deal was also met with criticism by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas, who echoed Zelensky in saying that suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
The deal with Russia is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average price of diesel is currently $6.28 (Â£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA â up from last month's $5.94 average, and $3.68 last year.
Under the deal, Russia would release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace" followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November.
A further million would follow, Trump wrote on Truth Social, and then another 3m tonnes "within a short period of time" â but he noted that this delivery will be "based on the condition of their diesel refineries".
In the past 10 months, Russia experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country due to Ukrainian drones strikes on its oil refineries.
Diesel production in Russia dropped by an estimated 30%, according to the International Energy Agency.
Trump had already called for new elections in Ukraine last December , external , saying Ukrainian voters should have the choice to replace Zelensky.
Since the war broke out in 2022 Ukraine has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.

Emergency Oil Releases Risk Draining the World’s Last Supply Cushion
The IEA is releasing another 100 million barrels of emergency oil and fuels, but global inventories are rapidly shrinking amid the prolonged Hormuz crisis.
The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to 331.2 million barrels, its lowest level since 1983, approaching the estimated operational minimum of 250–300 million barrels.
Aramco warns the global oil supply cushion is dangerously thin, with inventories potentially taking two years to replenish once Hormuz reopens, leaving markets vulnerable to further shocks.
Earlier this week, the International Energy Agency, after consulting with G7, said it would release another 100 million barrels of diesel, gasoline, and crude oil. The release is part of a plan announced in March to release 400 million barrels of oil in response to the Hormuz squeeze. But there is a problem with those releases—storage is emptying.
When the U.S. administration began releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, a flurry of reports followed, citing experts who warned the level of oil in the SPR was already low enough for concern, and any further draws would be risky. As of the start of October, the amount of oil in the strategic U.S. reserve stood at 331.2 million barrels, which was the lowest since 1983, following the latest release of over 9 million barrels. The releases are part of a 172-million-barrel release the United States committed to earlier this year.
The problem is that 331.2 million barrels is quite close to what experts say is the operational minimum for the storage system—between 250 and 300 million barrels. Letting oil levels fall near the operational minimum is dangerous because this begins to affect the storage infrastructure, and not in a good way. To avoid that, inventories need to be replenished—and to be able to respond to any future supply crunches, of course. Related: U.S. Oil Drilling Continues to Inch Upward
The U.S. strategic oil reserve, however, is not the only one reaching minimum levels. Global inventories are on the decline, too. According to the IEA’s latest monthly oil report , from September, global oil inventories dropped by 95 million barrels in August, bringing the total draws since February to 507 million barrels, translating into 2.8 million barrels daily. The one piece of good news that the IEA had in that report was that OECD commercial inventories rose by 23 million barrels, offsetting a 19-million-barrel draw in strategic reserves.
However, the good news did not last long. Earlier this week, Aramco’s chief executive Amin Nasser warned that the world’s oil inventories were running dangerously low—and implied the prospect of refilling them was rather distant.
“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “And, with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin.” The replenishment of drained inventories, Nasser noted, could take up to two years, and that only after the Strait of Hormuz reopens. While the world waits for that to happen, it is draining its inventories, exposing itself to much more severe supply shocks if the war drags on into 2027.
“IEA Member governments still have significant levels of publicly held emergency oil stocks – equivalent to around 1.1 billion barrels, including over 200 million barrels of diesel,” the agency’s head, Fatih Birol, said this week, following his meeting with agency members to discuss the new release of oil and fuel. “The IEA stands ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required.”
This was meant to reassure the market that there will be no shortage of, notably, diesel. However, it might well spark concern instead of allaying fears of shortages, because global inventories are also dangerously close to their operational minimum and that cannot be breached because once you breach it, you have no global inventory system.
The world has drawn over 1 billion barrels of crude from inventories since the start of the war between the United States and Israel, and Iran. Most of that came from commercial inventories, Aramco’s Nasser said this week. That leaves less than 6 billion barrels still in storage—and those 6 billion barrels are needed to stay where they are to keep the storage system functional. The world, it seems, has worn its oil supply cushion through.
No wonder, then, that a lot of countries, notably in Asia, are now in a race to build their oil inventories. Asia is especially vulnerable to adverse events in the Middle East because most of its oil imports come from the region. With that severely compromised, Asian economies, especially Southeast Asian ones, have been struggling to secure fuel for their economies and populations, and to keep them relatively affordable.
“The most advanced efforts are support for the development of oil stockpiling systems in each country and regional joint stockpiling on (a) voluntary basis,” nine governments from Southeast Asia said in a statement this week, as quoted by Reuters. In other words, they will be doing what the IEA is doing, to be able to better respond to future crises. But here is the thing—that oil that these countries will be stockpiling has to come from somewhere and not cost an arm and a leg. It would take a while before prices return to more palatable levels for Southeast Asian governments—or any other governments that would need to refill storage.

Putin relayed Iran war proposal to Trump, Kremlin says
Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's view on a possible resolution of the Iran conflict to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian state media reported.
The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Trump said Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement Trump said he agreed with Putin.
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska.
Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's vision for a possible end to the war in Iran to U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian state media reported Saturday.
The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin sent the message to Trump "in agreement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian," according to a Google translation.
Other Russian media reports said Putin spoke to Trump by  phone  after the Russian leader met Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan.
Interfax didn't elaborate on the specifics of how Iran sees the war — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets — coming to an end.
The White House didn't immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request to confirm the reported conversation between Putin and Trump.
Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement the U.S. president said he agreed with Putin during a phone call.
Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter, Trump said in a post on Truth Social . Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said.
The Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general license issued Friday.

Iran has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with vessels coming under fire almost daily as Tehran tries to choke off a rebound in crude exports.
A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency , an outlet considered close to the Guard.
The surge in attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, largely because the U.S. military escorted ships through Hormuz along Oman's coast.
An interim deal signed in June between the U.S. and Iran to pause hostilities to allow for negotiations quickly broke down.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately condemned Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Ukraine's leader warned that easing sanctions without a commitment from Russia to de-escalate the war will only prolong it.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in a social media post . "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
Diesel prices have surged worldwide as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports to global markets. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, further constraining fuel supplies.
Trump is under growing political pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Republicans face competitive elections in conservative strongholds like Iowa, where farmers feel the pinch of high diesel prices.

Nvidia built a $5 trillion company while making employees pay for their own lunch—but they get far more lucrative perks like stock discounts
Ship captains and crews transiting the Strait of Hormuz make so much danger pay that they’re ‘almost being viewed as mercenaries’
Iran's medium-sized oil tankers continue to wait off the coast of Bandar Abbas at the Strait of Hormuz in Hormozgan Province, Iran on September 9, 2026. Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images
The high-risk, high-reward business of moving oil through the Strait of Hormuz has gotten riskier and more rewarding.
Despite steady attacks from Iran, oil tankers and other commercial vessels have continued flowing through the narrow waterway. With protection from the U.S. military and help from pipelines bypassing the strait, Persian Gulf oil flows returned to prewar levels .
But seeking to reassert its leverage over the global oil chokepoint, Iran has stepped up drone and missile strikes on ships recently, including those outside the immediate vicinity of Hormuz.
While traffic has dipped in response, ships continue to cross, with many making shuttle runs in and out of the Gulf to unload oil cargoes via ship-to-ship transfers. Then other vessels deliver the barrels to customers.
For those onboard the ships willing to tolerate the risks in the Gulf, a hefty payday awaits. Tanker captains can earn $100,000 a month for transiting the strait, plus a $50,000 bonus for each trip, sources told the Financial Times .
That “danger money” is up from regular pay of about $15,000 a month, and is necessary for shipowners to keep their fleets crewed.
Meanwhile, sailors typically make at little as $1,500 a month. But trips through Hormuz can bump up earnings by at least four to six times their normal rates, the report said.
Other hot spots also offer hazard enhancements, albeit less than what’s available for Hormuz trips. According to the FT , captains and sailors get double pay in the southern Red Sea , where Houthis have been attacking Saudi ships, and in the Gulf of Oman, where many ship-to-ship transfers take place after Hormuz shuttle runs.
Because many ships and their crews are dedicated to the shuttle runs, they are in constant peril—allowing them to stack up all the bonuses and danger money for each trip.
A source told the FT that those brave enough to stomach the near-constant threat of attacks are “almost being viewed as mercenaries,” though some unwilling crew members are reportedly being pressured to stay onboard.
Since the Iran war started on Feb. 28, at least 93 ships have been hit, and 24 sailors have been killed, according to the International Maritime Organization.
In addition to the hazard pay for crews, shipowners are also paying for insurance, and the war risk can command 6%-10% of a ship’s value—translating to up to $20 million for a supertanker sailing through the Gulf.
All the added costs have made shipping expensive too. Freight rates for cargoes crossing the Strait of Hormuz hit a record high of $1.3 million per day, up from last year’s daily rate of $20,000-$50,000.
All the ships needed to get oil out of the Gulf have also contributed to a global tanker shortage that’s spiked freight rates around the world.
Shipbroker Gibson  pointed out that hiring a tanker to travel from the U.S. to China costs about $80 million, more than the $74 million price tag for a standard SpaceX Falcon 9 launch. Brokerage SSY estimated that rates are now the highest since the advent of the supertanker in the 1960s, even after adjusting for inflation.
Shipping costs have become so extreme that oil producers and even commodities traders are looking to own their own tankers to control the expenses.
But if freight costs get too high, they could erase the margins that can be earned from oil and refined fuels. For instance, European refiner Repsol saw its margin drop from $36 per barrel in the third quarter to $15 in October, according to analysts at RBC. Further reduction in margins could eventually force refiners to reduce how much crude they process.
The hazard premium could get worse in the Persian Gulf. Analysts have warned the Iranian regime, facing an existential threat to its rule, could re-escalate the war and take back its grip on the oil trade.
Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, founder and CEO of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation think tank, pointed out recently that Iran can still destroy regional oil infrastructure, such as drilling and refining capacity, and can escalate if President Donald Trump rejects diplomatic off-ramps.
“Iran did not wage a scorched earth campaign—but it may yet do so if the current situation persists for too long,”  he posted on X  late last month. “That is what everyone who actually follows this region and its dynamics is worried about.”

items.title: How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election
items.summary: Israel’s election signals not a demand for change, but deeper entrenchment of the jingoism unleashed after October 7.
items.content:
Share How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election on social media
Ultra-Orthodox Jewish men stand next to a billboard depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alongside leaders of opposition parties, with the slogan 'Right or Palestine', before Israel's general election, in Ashdod, Israel [Ohad Zwigenberg/AP]
As Israel entered the final month before its October 27 election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a chilling warning to share.
Israel’s enemies, he said on September 29, were plotting an attack on the country before the vote. Without providing any evidence, he then quickly referred to continuing attacks by Israeli troops in the Gaza Strip, where he said they had killed more than 100 “terrorists” in recent weeks.
That link drawn by Netanyahu – between the genocidal war on Gaza that began after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks, the upcoming elections, and Israel’s national security – was not coincidental, say analysts.
Netanyahu’s insistence that he alone can secure Israelis from a range of threats they face from across the country’s borders, they say, lies at the heart of his re-election campaign, even as his alleged failures during the attack three years ago and in securing the quick release of captives have offered his opponents ammunition.
When a Flydubai flight packed with Israeli passengers on their way from Dubai to Tel Aviv a day after his recent warning nearly crashed after a co-pilot attacked his pilot with an axe in the cockpit, Netanyahu was quick to seize on the incident to argue that he is still man for the country’s top job.
Polls suggest that he faces a stiff test in what is the first general vote since the 2023 attacks, which led to the killing of 1,139 people in Israel and triggered the genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, where Israeli have attacks have since killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
Three years later, the war has become inseparable from the domestic debate over Israel’s direction while also accelerating a political shift to the right – with once-fringe positions on Palestinians now very much the mainstream view.
Few embody this transformation more than Israel’s far-right financial Minister Bezalel Smotrich, sanctioned by a number of Western countries and known for his incendiary and racist language and policies towards Palestinians.
In one of his characteristically inflammatory statements , Smotrich told Israeli outlet Ynet late last month that the Israeli army should “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and “do there what we did in Gaza”.
Less than two weeks later, Smotrich’s electoral ally Moshe Feiglin added fuel to the fire.
“The enemy is Gaza, not Hamas”, he told the Jerusalem Post, calling for the annexation of the besieged territory after the election. “The baby that will be born tomorrow in Gaza will do exactly the same,” he said, in reference to the 2023 attacks.
Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar said these are not “stray comments” from marginal figures but an electoral message from power-seeking politicians aimed at portraying Palestinians as “not a people with rights, but a demographic and security problem to be expelled, conquered or destroyed”.
He added: “The frightening reality is that the coming election risks becoming a competition not over whether Palestinian life should be protected, but over who can promise to erase it most aggressively.”
Following October 7, the younger generation in particular slid rightwards, said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.
He said the forces driving Israel to the right had been gathering for decades.
“The trend toward the right began after the Yom Kippur War in 1973, but it has intensified dramatically since October 7,” Bregman told Al Jazeera, referring to the bloody 19-day October War , or the 1973 Arab-Israeli War – a conflict between Israel and a coalition of Arab states led by Egypt and Syria.
More recently, the far right has been emboldened through electoral politics as part of Netanyahu’s government since 2022 – the most right-wing government in Israeli history.
Another outspoken cabinet member alongside Smotrich is Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir , a far-right provocateur who has previously been convicted of inciting racism and of supporting a terrorist organisation.
“Netanyahu’s greatest mistake – among many – was bringing figures like Ben-Gvir and Smotrich into his coalition,” said Bergman. “By doing so, he legitimised them as influential forces in Israeli politics.”
Ben-Gvir has been so cemented into Israel’s political system, he has hopes pinned on becoming the next Israeli defence minister, the analyst pointed out.
“This is madness. But that’s contemporary Israel,” said Bergman.
Attendees listen and applaud during an election campaign meeting on October 5, 2026 in Tel Aviv, Israel [Erik Marmor/Getty Images] Analysts also pointed out that several parties running, including ones that are currently in power and a number that are challenging the current coalition, all advocate for the expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza, as one of the examples of the shift to the right.
Omar Baddar, director of Palthink for Strategic Studies, said the messaging from across the Israeli political and military spectrum in the lead-up to the election shows that there is “a consensus” to continue the attacks on Gaza, where nearly 1,500 have been killed since a “ceasefire” last year.
“They’re using the threats to get more votes,” he said, pointing out to what he described as the radicalisation of the society.
With the election approaching, added Baddar, Israeli leaders are seeking to undo one another: “Who[ever]’s more radical is more likely to get more votes.”
As Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher from inside Israel, writes , “what it means to be ‘right-wing’ in Israel today is above all to take a harder line on Palestinian national claims, security and territorial control.”
He adds: “On security and the Palestinians, a large part of Jewish Israeli politics already works from assumptions that would have been treated as right-wing a generation ago: Deep suspicion of a sovereign Palestinian state, a high tolerance for prolonged military control, and a stronger insistence on Jewish sovereignty as the starting point rather than one value among others.”
Observers and rights groups say the disparity is even evident in the electoral process. A prominent politician and Palestinian citizen of Israel, Sami Abu Shehadeh, has been forced to withdraw from the election over his remarks about the Gaza war, while Israeli far-right leaders have remained untouched despite their violent rhetoric against Palestinians.
Recent polling indicates that the events of October 7 are top of mind for Israelis, who also have questions about who was responsible for the security failures of that day.
Just last month, reports surfaced indicating that Netanyahu had received two separate warnings about an imminent Hamas attack in 2023, from Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, and United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Netanyahu’s two main rivals in the race for prime minister have cited the alleged warnings to call the prime minister “unfit” to remain at the helm of the country.
But Netanyahu has denied suggestions that he had been forewarned about the attack, and the reports do not appear to have had a significant effect on opinion polls.
While October 7 represents a profound rupture in Israelis’ sense of security, public trust in the Netanyahu government had already been badly shaken by its controversial judicial overhaul , introduced when the prime minister’s current coalition first came to power, said Mairav Zonszein, an Israel-Palestine analyst at the International Crisis Group based in Tel Aviv.
Despite these breaches of trust, the Israeli leader retains support.
“Israelis in general still see Netanyahu as kind of the guy on security. And more to the point, they don’t really see an alternative,” Zonszein told Al Jazeera.
A June survey by Mitvim – the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies found that the Israeli public supports its government’s military and security solutions, and rejects resolving the Palestinian issue and ending the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory. This is the case even while it has been concerned about international isolation and the decline of Israel’s international standing since the beginning of the genocidal war on Gaza, the survey reported.
Yet Israelis are also increasingly war-weary, even as they back the use of more force. Its troops – stretched between six fronts of war in the last few years – are bearing the brunt of this fatigue in Israeli society.
Israel’s Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday that nearly 30,000 soldiers and security personnel are facing psychological trauma since the war.
The ministry said its rehabilitation department’s budget has increased by 88 percent over the past three years to 10 billion shekels ($3.3m), with the majority supporting treatment for mental health conditions and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Still, Israel in recent months has been more and more vocal about its expansionist vision, with officials brazenly stating the goal of “ Greater Israel ”. The claim for the conquest is based on a biblical verse (Genesis 15:18-21).
For decades, Israel has ignored international law in its continuous occupation of Palestinian and Syrian land, and has shown little respect for its neighbours’ sovereignty, occupying more land in Syria, as well as in Lebanon in more recent years.
According to Najar, the political economist, the “complete dehumanisation” of Palestinians as evidenced during the campaign reveal that Gaza “is being presented to Israeli voters not as a catastrophe or a crime for which there must be accountability, but as a blueprint to be repeated elsewhere”.
In southern Lebanon, where Israel has been carrying out near daily attacks and and has occupied large swathes of land, residents have told Al Jazeera they expect little to change even if Netanyahu is defeated in the election.
Netanyahu’s main political challenger, Gadi Eisenkot – head of the Yashar party and former army chief of staff – is the father of the so-called Dahiyeh Doctrine, and is just as hawkish about expansion. That doctrine, since Israel’s war with the Lebanese group Hezbollah in 2006, calls for the use of huge force, even against civilian infrastructure, as a deterrent against enemies and was deployed in Israel’s recent wars, particularly in Beirut’s southern suburbs.
If it were up to Eisenkot, the Lebanon front of war would have never scaled down: He has accused Netanyahu of bowing to US pressure to halt operations in Beirut, and has insisted that the military should be able to attack Hezbollah anywhere in Lebanon.
For Israelis still reeling from the events of October 7, Eisenkot could fill the security void many are feeling, said Zonszein.
“They really … see the world as kind of very hostile towards them, the world not understanding what they went through on October 7, and [therefore why] the need to have these security buffer zones in Lebanon, in Syria, and Gaza,” she said.
A two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict is therefore out of the question, said the analysts – and has not even made a blip of an appearance in campaigning before the election.
The idea first emerged during the Oslo Accords more than 30 years ago, which set out a negotiating process aimed at resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, predicated on the belief that the creation of a Palestinian state alongside Israel was imperative to forge peace.
But since the Oslo process began in 1993, the number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank has ballooned from about 260,000 to more than 700,000, embedded deep inside West Bank areas that would be needed for a contiguous Palestinian state.
“The concept of a two-state solution is currently irrelevant and likely will remain so for another decade or two, if not longer,” said Bergman. “It is unlikely to become a reality in the foreseeable future, as no Israeli leader can propose it to the Israeli public after the events of October 7.”
The only way it could regain prominence is if there is substantial international pressure, including severe sanctions on Israel, and a non-violent intifada, or an uprising by Palestinians, he said.
The outright rejection of Palestinian statehood has simply become much more “acceptable”, said Zonszein.
“There’s several parties who advocate these views, whereas there isn’t a single Jewish Zionist Party that puts the need for a two-state solution or a Palestinian political process at the forefront,” she said.
Taken all together, Israel’s election appears less a demand for change than a further entrenchment of the jingoism that surged after October 7, 2023.
“[There’s] more and more movement towards more military force, more need for pushing the borders … out of a lot of fear that another October 7 could happen,” said Zonszein.

items.summary: Moscow and Washington tout a diesel deal to ease sanctions and reopen fuel flows, but few details leave questions on price impacts and U.S. policy, sparking anger from Ukraine and allies.
items.content:
U.S. and Russia tout diesel deal to ease sanctions and reopen fuel flows Moscow and Washington tout a diesel deal to ease sanctions and reopen fuel flows, but few details leave questions on price impacts and U.S. policy, sparking anger from Ukraine and allies.
U.S. and Russia tout diesel deal to ease sanctions and reopen fuel flows
U.S. and Russia tout diesel deal to ease sanctions and reopen fuel flows
< iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5996938/nx-s1-9959708" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Moscow and Washington tout a diesel deal to ease sanctions and reopen fuel flows, but few details leave questions on price impacts and U.S. policy, sparking anger from Ukraine and allies.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST: President Trump says the U.S. will begin to import Russian diesel to try to drive down gas prices before the midterm elections. The U.S. had banned Russian diesel to limit Russia's revenue amid the war in Ukraine. NPR's Russia correspondent Charles Maynes joins us from Moscow. Charles, thanks for being with us. CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott. SIMON: And tell us, please, about the president's announcement. I gather it was on social media. MAYNES: Yeah. That's right. Trump revealed the news on his Truth Social platform. He wrote that he'd had a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin of Russia whereby Putin agreed to immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets, with more to follow. Trump said this meant diesel prices for Americans and for the rest of the world would be coming down - in his words - in record numbers and fast. That was in all caps. And he said he did this with certain constituencies in mind, saying farmers, ranchers and truckers were his greatest priority. Those, of course, are some of the groups who have been unhappy about the rise in diesel prices and who Trump will need to turn out in the midterms if Republicans are going to hold the House, much less the Senate. SIMON: It is an election year. Politics might be driving U.S. economic policy abroad? MAYNES: That's right - at least for now. The U.S. formally placed sanctions on Russia - Russian diesel shortly after the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022. And it just took minutes after Trump's announcement for the Treasury Department to issue a six-month waiver to those trade restrictions. SIMON: Charles, how would a deal actually work? MAYNES: Oddly enough, this requires Russia to first lift its own diesel export ban. The Kremlin put that restriction in place in response to gas shortages that have hit Russia over the summer due to sustained Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian energy facilities. That crisis has basically eased a bit. So this deal comes at a moment, really, when industry experts here were already calling for the lifting of this ban on exports to other parts of the world, saying Russia was basically losing out on profit. And this U.S. deal to lift sanctions certainly helps them do this - just quicker, maybe, than some thought. SIMON: And how are the leaders of Russia talking about the deal? MAYNES: Well, the Kremlin issued a more general statement than Trump, saying it was ready to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets, kind of full stop. But clearly, part of the story behind this deal is the warm relationship between Trump and Putin. A Kremlin adviser, Yuri Ushakov, later described to journalists the atmosphere of this call, saying Trump had wished Putin a happy birthday - Putin turned 74 this week and said, even, that neither side wanted to put down the phone despite taking a call for an hour and a half. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) YURI USHAKOV: (Speaking Russian). MAYNES: Here's Ushakov saying he hoped Trump wouldn't mind if he quoted him, but that the U.S. president had told Putin he was ready to talk more today, more tonight or any day after. So these guys really seem to like each other. SIMON: And how much will importing Russian oil actually affect prices in the U.S.? MAYNES: Well, the Russian contribution to the global diesel needs in the short term isn't that much. And industry experts say, actually, it isn't likely to have the immediate impact that Trump says or is promising for diesel prices at the pump. How that impacts voters' decisions in November, of course, we'll have to see. But the other interest here for Trump is Ukraine. You know, Trump has actually blamed Ukraine for driving up prices at the pump through its attacks on Russian energy facilities, even though most experts would say that while that may be a factor, the real cause has been Iran's blockage of the Strait of Hormuz. Be that as it may, Trump has been pressuring Ukraine to unilaterally halt its attacks on Russia to help with these gas prices, something Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has thus far refused to do without a reciprocal move by Moscow. SIMON: How has President Zelenskyy reacted to news that Russia and the U.S. are striking this deal? MAYNES: Well, he clearly doesn't like it. He said that the White House's decision prolongs the war by replenishing Russia's war chest. Here's Zelenskyy speaking in a voice message to reporters last night. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) PRESIDENT VOLODYMYR ZELENSKYY: (Speaking Ukrainian). MAYNES: So here Zelenskyy says the deal means more money for this war and more money to inflict suffering on Ukrainians, adding it only feeds Putin's ability to keep fighting. You know, and left unsaid, this deal gives Trump even more incentive to pressure Kyiv to halt its attacks on Russian energy, even as Putin continues his attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure - you know, on homes, on heating, electrical power stations - as we enter into the winter months with Ukraine's air defenses depleted. SIMON: NPR's Russia correspondent Charles Maynes. Thanks so much. MAYNES: Thank you.

Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 10, 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin used his phone call with US President Donald Trump on October 9 to falsely blame Ukraine for the lack of peace negotiations’ progress despite Russia’s continued unwillingness to engage in meaningful negotiations or make any concessions to end the war in Ukraine. Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov claimed that Putin told Trump that Ukraine’s alleged long-range strikes against Russian election infrastructure during the September 2026 Russian State Duma elections “thwarted the possibility” of “immediately” resuming peace negotiations — attempting to malign Ukraine as the party responsible for halting peace negotiations.[1] There is, in fact, no evidence that Ukraine targeted Russian election infrastructure during the September 2026 Duma elections, and Russian claims that Ukraine attempted to target election infrastructure remain unfounded. Putin emphasized that Russia’s commitment to achieve all its war goals and objectives — which are tantamount to full Ukrainian and Western surrender — remain unchanged. Ukraine, the United States, and Europe have repeatedly presented various ceasefires and peace proposals with concessions to Russia — all of which the Kremlin has continuously rejected.[2] Moscow has insisted on painting Ukraine as the intransigent party in peace efforts despite the fact that Russia has not offered any concessions and has rejected numerous compromise proposals that the US and Ukraine have offered. Putin’s October 9 reiteration of his commitment to Russia’s unchanged war aims demonstrates the Kremlin’s continued unwillingness to accept any compromised peace proposals on any terms that fall short of fulfilling Russia’s maximalist demands of Ukraine’s complete capitulation.[3]
The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) is presenting a tailored weekly summary of the Russian forces’ exaggerated military successes aimed specifically at Russia’s domestic audience through Max – the new social media platform that the Russian state has developed to control the Russian internet. The Russian MoD published a rollup of Russian claimed battlefield successes on October 9 only on its Max channel, a Russian messenger platform which requires Russian or Belarusian phone numbers as a prerequisite for registration, and claimed that Russian forces seized two settlements in Ukraine between October 3 and 9 and another three over the past 24 hours.[4] The Russian MoD also claimed that Russian forces thwarted Ukrainian forces' attempts to conduct rotations or break out of the claimed encirclements in Dobropillya, Donetsk Oblast, and near Chorne (northeast of Kharkiv City).[5] The Russian MoD claimed that the Russian Northern Grouping of Forces (GoF) seized 414 square kilometers and 20 settlements since encircling Ukrainian forces in Kharkiv Oblast — an exaggerated claim that has no basis in reality, as Ukrainian forces and Russian milbloggers themselves have refuted or questioned claims that Russian forces encircled any Ukrainian forces in northern Kharkiv Oblast.[6] The MoD rollup also highlighted the Russian long-range strikes against defense industry facilities, telecommunications centers, and dry cargo ships in Ukraine over the past week.[7] The Russian MoD notably only published this weekly summary on its Max channel rather than on its internationally-facing Telegram channel, indicating that the Russian MoD likely aims to highlight and exaggerate the Russian forces’ weekly military achievements specifically for the Russian domestic audience and present Russian continuing battlefield successes despite evidence that Russian advances have significantly slowed.[8] The apparent difference in messaging suggests that the Kremlin seeks to minimize the amount of international scrutiny it receives from its baseless claims of Russian successes, though the MoD still makes highly exaggerated claims on its Telegram channel — claims that ISW regularly refutes.[9]

Russia's Winter 2026-2027 strike campaign against Ukraine's energy grid is trying in part to damage Ukraine's infrastructure for transmitting electricity between regions. Ukrainian state energy company Ukrenergo reported on October 9 that Russian forces are using a new strike tactic to degrade Ukraine's energy grid — continuous strikes on substations, transmission lines, and distribution systems, especially near large cities that consume high quantities of electricity.[54] Russian forces are systematically destroying power generation facilities in some Ukrainian oblasts, leading to energy shortages in those areas and forcing Ukrainian authorities to transmit electricity from other regions hundreds of kilometers away. Ukrenergo noted that continuous Russian strikes and air raid sirens complicate efforts to rapidly repair and restore damaged energy infrastructure. A multi-part Russian plan for the Winter 2026-2027 strike campaign, which Western media outlets recently reviewed and publicized, also calls for Russian strikes to disable substations, transmission lines, and interconnectors near Ukraine's western border through which Ukraine imports European electricity.[55] Russia's Winter 2025-2026 strike campaign also targeted Ukraine's transmission and distribution infrastructure.[56]

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
US President Donald Trump told reporters on October 10 that he is considering whether the United States will conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis in response to recent Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and other civilian infrastructure.
The Houthis are attacking several Yemeni government positions south and west of Taiz City in an effort to fully encircle and capture the city, while Yemeni government-aligned forces continue to stall the Houthi advances.
US President Donald Trump told reporters on October 10 that he is considering whether the United States will conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis in response to recent Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and other civilian infrastructure.[1] The Houthis almost certainly conducted a missile attack on October 10 targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which the group has attacked several times in recent days.[2] A regional official told the Associated Press on October 10 that a missile struck a terminal complex at the airport and wounded many people.[3] The Houthis have expanded the scale of ballistic missile, cruise missile, and drone attacks targeting Saudi civilian airports since Yemeni government-aligned forces launched a counteroffensive to retake territory on the Red Sea coastal plain on October 4.[4] The Houthis' frequent attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure, particularly airports, are currently motivating Saudi efforts to degrade Houthi ballistic missile capabilities and other long-range strike platforms.
Potential US involvement in the Saudi-Yemeni government air campaign to degrade Houthi ballistic missile capabilities would mark the first direct US military action against the group since the conclusion of Operation Rough Rider in May 2025.[5] US strikes during Operation Rough Rider degraded Houthi missile and other strike capabilities that the group used to attack civilian vessels in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandeb Strait.[6] The United States and other partner forces have expanded military assistance, including intelligence, targeting, and air defense support, to Saudi Arabia in recent weeks.[7] These forms of military assistance support Saudi efforts to inhibit Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia by exposing Houthi strike capabilities to Saudi air assets and protecting civilian infrastructure from Houthi missiles and drones.
The Houthis are attacking several Yemeni government positions south and west of Taiz City in an effort to fully encircle and capture the city, while Yemeni government-aligned forces continue to stall the Houthi advances. Yemeni military sources told joint UK-Emirati media on October 10 that Yemeni government-aligned forces repelled an attempted Houthi advance in the vicinity of Wadi al Dhabab, which is a valley located on the southwestern outskirts of Taiz City.[8] The sources also reported that Houthi fighters have engaged Yemeni government-aligned forces in heavy combat in the vicinities of Jabal Sabr and Najd Qasim, which are both located less than 10 kilometers south of Taiz City.[9] Yemeni media also reported on October 10 that Yemeni government-aligned forces repelled an attempted Houthi advance in the vicinity of al Shaqab, which is located about 12 kilometers south of Taiz City.[10] The Houthis claimed on October 10 that the group is securing control over central Taiz Governorate's Mawasit, Sama, and al Salu districts.[11] ISW-CTP has not observed verifiable reports that corroborate the Houthis’ claim at the time of this writing. The Houthis' attempted advances on several fronts south and west of Taiz City indicate that the group is preparing to fully encircle and attempt to capture the city, which is Yemen's third largest city.[12]
These attempted Houthi advances come amid Houthi efforts to consolidate and secure ground lines of communication (GLOC) leading into Taiz City from peripheral areas of Taiz Governorate. Houthi Taiz "Governor" Ahmed al Masawi announced on October 9 that the group has reopened several roadways in Taiz Governorate for civilian use, including the Mokha-Najd al Nashamah roadway and other roads in central and southern Taiz Governorate.[13] This official announcement indicates that the Houthis assess that they have secured sufficient control over the roadways and surrounding terrain to permit relatively normal civilian and economic activity to resume. Masawi also characterized the Houthis’ decision to reopen roads to Taiz City as a humanitarian issue and urged civilians in government-held areas to reopen remaining roads and permit the flow of civilian necessities into Taiz City.[14] Masawi’s comments are likely intended to weaken Yemeni government-aligned forces’ and anti-Houthi civilians’ will to resist Houthi control over Taiz City, particularly as the group’s encirclement of central Taiz Governorate is exacerbating critical supply shortages in government-held areas.[15]
Houthi control of terrain surrounding key GLOCs leading to Taiz City does not insulate the group's logistics from Saudi and Yemeni government attacks, however. Saudi and Yemeni government drones and warplanes have targeted Houthi reinforcements, weapons depots, and logistical centers behind Houthi lines in Taiz Governorate in recent weeks in order to deprive Houthi frontline forces of necessary sustainment.[16] The high volume of recent Saudi and Yemeni government airstrikes and drone strikes on Houthi targets attests to these forces' air superiority throughout Yemen, which the Houthis have largely failed to disrupt.[17]
The Saudi-Yemeni government air campaign also intends to degrade the Houthis' long-range strike capabilities and support Yemeni government-aligned forces on frontlines across Yemen. Saudi Joint Forces Command (JFC) spokesperson Major General Turki al Maliki announced on October 9 that Saudi forces have recently destroyed 136 Houthi military targets in Yemen and that JFC intends to destroy the Houthis' ballistic missile capabilities.[18] Saudi forces have conducted numerous airstrikes targeting Houthi ballistic missile launchers and missile storage sites, which are critical to the group's ability to target Saudi civilian infrastructure and Yemeni government-aligned forces' staging areas, across Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen in recent days.[19] Maliki added that the JFC is providing 24-hour close air support coverage to Yemeni government-aligned forces.[20]

Putin relayed Iran war proposal to Trump, Kremlin says
Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's view on a possible resolution of the Iran conflict to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian state media reported.
The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Trump said Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement Trump said he agreed with Putin.
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska.
Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's vision for a possible end to the war in Iran to U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian state media reported Saturday.
The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin sent the message to Trump "in agreement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian," according to a Google translation.
Other Russian media reports said Putin spoke to Trump by  phone  after the Russian leader met Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan.
Interfax didn't elaborate on the specifics of how Iran sees the war — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets — coming to an end.
The White House didn't immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request to confirm the reported conversation between Putin and Trump.
Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement the U.S. president said he agreed with Putin during a phone call.
Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter, Trump said in a post on Truth Social . Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said.
The Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general license issued Friday.
Brent crude oil price, U.S. dollars per barrel, year to date
Iran has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with vessels coming under fire almost daily as Tehran tries to choke off a rebound in crude exports.
A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency , an outlet considered close to the Guard.
The surge in attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, largely because the U.S. military escorted ships through Hormuz along Oman's coast.
An interim deal signed in June between the U.S. and Iran to pause hostilities to allow for negotiations quickly broke down.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately condemned Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Ukraine's leader warned that easing sanctions without a commitment from Russia to de-escalate the war will only prolong it.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in a social media post . "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
Diesel prices have surged worldwide as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports to global markets. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, further constraining fuel supplies.
Trump is under growing political pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Republicans face competitive elections in conservative strongholds like Iowa, where farmers feel the pinch of high diesel prices.

items.content:
Outsize stock market returns have been a theme with President Donald Trump in the White House. The iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.83% ) , benchmark S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.59% ) , and innovation-driven Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC +0.64% ) rallied 57%, 70%, and 142%, respectively, during his first non-consecutive term, and have gained 18%, 30%, and 40% since the start of his second term.
Trump's presidency has benefited from the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, better-than-expected corporate earnings, and record S&P 500 share repurchases. The latter has been fueled by the president's flagship tax-and-spending law from his first term, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which permanently lowered the peak marginal corporate income tax rate to 21%.
Image source: Official White House Photo by Patrick B. Ruddy.
But things may not be as rosy as Wall Street's major stock indexes indicate. Although history can't concretely predict what's to come, past events have a knack for foreshadowing big moves in the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite.
Right now, two prediction tools, neither of which has ever been wrong, point to a significant forthcoming decline in stocks under President Trump.
A historically pricey stock market portends disaster
Perhaps the most visible concern for the bull market that's flourished under President Trump since his second term inauguration is stock valuations.
Valuing individual stocks and the broader market is particularly tricky because there isn't a step-by-step blueprint for doing so. Investors' emotions and subjectivity often come into play, making it especially challenging to predict short-term directional moves in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite.
But the one time-tested valuation tool that's demonstrated its ability to cut through this emotion and subjectivity is the S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio ( CAPE Ratio ). Currently, the Shiller P/E Ratio is making dubious history.
Stock Market Shiller PE Ratio on the verge of taking out its Dot Com Bubble all-time high 🚨 🤯 👀 https://t.co/CtCmSgWnLt
Though economists introduced the Shiller P/E less than 40 years ago, it's been backtested nearly 156 years to January 1871. Over this time frame, the Shiller P/E Ratio has averaged 17.42. As of the closing bell on Oct. 7, this premier valuation tool had a multiple of 41.80, with the evolution of AI powering stock valuations into the stratosphere.
Over the last 156 years, the CAPE Ratio has exceeded 30 for at least two consecutive months only six times , including the present. The previous five instances all portended disaster for the stock market. Premium valuations were observed before the start of the Great Depression and the bursting of the dot-com bubble. The Great Depression wiped away 89% of the Dow's value, while the dot-com bubble slashed the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite by 49% and 78% , respectively.
History shows that premium stock valuations aren't sustainable over an extended timeline. While the CAPE Ratio can't pinpoint when the music will stop, nor can it guarantee that a stock market crash will occur, it has successfully portended five significant downturns over the last century.
In other words, the second-priciest CAPE Ratio in history increases the odds that the stock market crashes under Donald Trump.
Risk-taking has gone parabolic, and that's terrible news for stocks
However, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio isn't the only predictive tool that has a flawless track record of foreshadowing the future. One of Wall Street's crudest measures of risk-taking, outstanding margin debt, is also sending all the wrong signals.
Margin represents the money an investor borrows from their broker, with interest, to wager against (short-sell) or purchase securities. If margin is used to purchase a stock, it acts as a form of leverage and is therefore a crude measure of an investor's willingness to take risks .
On the one hand, if a security moves in the desired direction, margin can amplify an investor's gains. But if it moves opposite to what was expected, margin debt can quickly magnify losses. When coupled with owing interest, using margin can be quite risky.
Nevertheless, outstanding margin debt across all brokers, reported monthly by FINRA, is expected to steadily rise over time in lockstep with the overall stock market. In those rare instances when outstanding margin debt goes parabolic (i.e., when risk-taking dramatically increases), history shows that things tend to break.
BREAKING: US margin debt surged +$37 billion in August, to $1.45 trillion, its 2nd-highest on record.
Margin debt has risen +$228 billion year-to-date, or +19%.
Since the end of 2022, investor borrowing has soared a massive +$847 billion, or +140%.
This has significantly outpaced the S&P 500's gain of +98% over the same period.
At the same time, margin debt as a % of GDP has almost doubled, to a record 4.5%.
By comparison, the 2021 and 2000 Dot-Com Bubble highs were 3.6% and 2.8%, respectively.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) September 17, 2026
Over the last 30 years, there have been four instances, including the present, in which outstanding margin debt has surged by at least 65% over a relatively short time frame :
March 1999 to March 2000 : Margin debt up 80% to nearly $300 billion
June 2006 to July 2007 : Margin debt soared 66% to around $416 billion
March 2020 to October 2021 : Margin debt skyrocketed 95% to roughly $936 billion
April 2025 to June 2026 : Margin debt surged 77% to a record $1.502 trillion
The previous three events immediately preceded the bursting of the dot-com bubble, the financial crisis, and the 2022 bear market.
When risk-taking soars, to borrow a phrase from Warren Buffett, the "time to be fearful when others are greedy" has arrived .
Although outstanding margin debt, like the Shiller P/E Ratio, can't tell us precisely when downturns will begin or if these downturns will come in the form of a stock market crash, surging margin debt has historically correlated with some short-lived crash events. It would appear that the odds of a stock market crash under President Trump are rising.

Former Bank of Korea governor Rhee Chang-yong said, "People say the semiconductor cycle lasts 10 years, but there is a worry it might end in just a few years."
The former governor appeared on YouTube's "SUKA World" on the 10th and said, "The current strength in semiconductors reflects the competitiveness of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, but it is also affected by China faltering because, due to U.S.-China tensions, it has been unable to import Netherlands-based ASML's lithography equipment."

The former governor also voiced concern about the government's expansionary fiscal policy. He said, "The Bank of Korea (BOK)'s growth forecast for next year is 2.9%, and there is a question of whether we really need to use fiscal spending to push the rate even higher." He added, "If this year's growth surges due to fiscal effects, next year's growth could be that much lower because of the base effect," and said, "Even if the semiconductor cycle improves, it does not solve the low birthrate and aging problems."
Regarding the second transfer of public institutions to the provinces, he said, "Rather than merely dispersing institutions across some regions, we should concentrate capabilities in a specific region to create a 'counterweight to Seoul.'" items.title: Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
items.summary: A desperate junta is in a war of attrition against ethnic militias and and civilian resistance.
items.content:
Image caption, Authorities in Myanmar have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas, leading to corruption, extortion and abductions
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.
"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.
"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."
Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.
According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.
Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says â to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.
Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.
The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.
Image caption, An estimated 100,000 young recruits have been conscriptedby the junta since early 2024
Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years â many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.
"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.
The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.
With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.
The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription â either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen â the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.
International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.
In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.
Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.
"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.
Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.
Figure caption, Watch: BBC goes into jungle with Myanmar's civil war rebels
"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."
Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.
"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."
Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.
The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; Â£680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.
In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.
U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.
When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.
But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.
"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.
"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.
Image caption, Ma Moe San Pan says her husband was sold into military service by her own cousin
In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.
The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.
Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.
Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.
"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."
In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department â a branch of the home affairs ministry â and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.
The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.
BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.
"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.
"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."
Image caption, It's been more than a year since Ma Moe San Pan last saw her husband Phyo Wai
While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper â demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population â wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.
So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.
Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".
But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.
It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.
The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".
In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.
Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.
As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."

items.title: Expedition hopes to find aviator Amelia Earhart's plane on remote island
items.summary: The team en route to the suspected crash site aim finally to solve the mystery of her 1937 disappearance.
items.content:
Image caption, The research team departed Kiribati's capital on Wednesday and hope to arrive at the suspected wreck site by Monday
A team of researchers are on their way to a remote island to inspect what they think could be the plane wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.
The group, from the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean by Monday in the hopes of solving the mystery of her disappearance.
The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation on her fate.
The team are aiming to find what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020.
Purdue University said the object had since been confirmed to have been visible in aerial photography of the area dating back to 1938.
The researchers are currently roughly halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard the Marin Mainiku, a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel.
They departed the capital of Kiribati on Wednesday to begin the 830-mile journey to Nikumaroro, which is also part of the multi-island country.
When they eventually arrive, they will have to navigate through a narrow gap created in the atoll's reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.
"Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the ALI and the expedition lead, said.
Image caption, A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on Nikumaroro
Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.
From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.
But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.
Earhart's disappearance spawned numerous theories - from a simple crash due to fuel exhaustion to more elaborate claims of interference.
The official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems while the two struggled to find the island, and Earhart eventually crashed into the ocean when she ran out of fuel.
While this version of events is largely accepted, no physical evidence has ever been recovered.
Image caption, Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937
One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.
Images of the so-called Taraia Object show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.
But some - including rival explorers - have expressed scepticism that this could be a plane, let alone Earhart's.
Ric Gillespie, who specialises in recovering historic aircraft wrecks, told news agency Reuters that the object looked like a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the nearby water.
"I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," he said.
The researchers en route to the island credit Gillespie with previously finding evidence of a human presence on the atoll in the 1930s and forensic analysis of skeletal remains found there in the 1940s they say lend credence to their theory.
But Gillespie suspects Earhart's plane had likely broken apart and its fragments carried into the depths of the Pacific long ago.
Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.
In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.
Similarly, an expedition in 2019, conducted by the marine archaeologist who discovered the Titanic wreck, to investigate a photograph of what might have been a landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.
