Like Meta's Muse AI Agents? 4 AI Semiconductor Stocks Set to Benefit From the Rise of AI Agents.
Meta Platforms ' (NASDAQ: META) artificial intelligence (AI) Muse agents have taken the world by storm. After being introduced just last month, Muse already has roughly 2 million daily active users as of Oct. 5 and sits atop the most downloaded apps on Apple 's (NASDAQ: AAPL) App Store. With consumer, enterprise, and small-business AI agents, the agentic AI market is set to explode.
But before AI agents take over the world, they will need many more central processing units (CPUs) to power them. While graphics processing units (GPUs) are used to train AI models and run inference , what they are not good at is providing the sequential logic required by AI agents.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
That is where server CPUs come in. As such, the ratio of GPUs to CPUs is expected to drop from 8:1 for AI model training and 4:1 for inference to 1:1 for servers dedicated to AI agents.
Image source: Getty Images. As a result, Bank of America has projected that the data center CPU market will grow from around $61.4 billion this year to $210.6 billion in 2030. That is pretty consistent with the $220 billion projections that both Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) have placed on the server CPU market.
Let's look at the four semiconductor stocks set to benefit the most from the agentic AI uprising.
The company set to benefit most from the rise of agentic AI and the surge in server CPU demand is arguably Arm Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM). It derives revenue from the server CPU market in two ways. First, it provides the IP (intellectual property) through licensing and subscriptions for nearly all custom CPUs. Meanwhile, earlier this year, it announced it would start making its own server CPUs for the first time.
Bank of America projects that custom Arm-based chips can capture nearly 38% of the server CPU market in 2030, while Arm's new mass-market chip will take a 9.4% market share.
On the downside, the company is also highly tied to the smartphone market, which is seeing unit declines due to price increases related to higher component costs, specifically memory. However, its server CPU market should more than make up for this.
AMD is one of the leaders in the server CPU market, having consistently taken share from rival Intel (NASDAQ: AMD) over the past few years. The company has already designed high-performance CPUs with high core counts specifically for agentic AI workloads and looks well-positioned to continue taking market share.
While the company has said it is looking to capture a 50% market share, Bank of America estimates AMD's market share will climb from 27.7% this year to 30.7% in 2030.
AMD also has a big opportunity in AI inference with its GPUs, which should be a second big growth driver.
Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) is the current market share leader in the data center CPU space with an over 40% share in 2025. As such, it has seen a sudden burst of revenue growth, given that the market is supply-constrained. This has allowed it to sell older-generation CPUs and also raise prices.
However, Bank of America projects that its market share will drop to around 22% by 2030. It also has a money-losing foundry business that has been like a weight around the company's neck. After some huge gains this year, Intel is my least favorite way to play the current CPU megatrend.
While best known for its GPUs, Nvidia has also developed its own Arm-based CPUs. It sells these as stand-alone chips, packaged with its GPUs, and as parts of entire server racks.
While this positions Nvidia to get its fair share of this booming market, its GPU revenue ultimately overwhelms its CPU opportunity. Expect GPUs and complete end-to-end server systems to be the main drivers of the company's growth moving forward. It's still a great stock, but just one that benefits a little less from this opportunity, given the difference in size between the GPU and CPU markets.

items.content:

Ben Roberts-Smith attends Canberra event honouring Australian troops who served in Afghanistan
Anthony Albanese speaks at Australian War Memorial event commemorating 25th anniversary of country’s involvement in the conflict
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Anthony Albanese has honoured Australian troops who served in Afghanistan, using the 25th anniversary of the country’s involvement in the conflict to describe their heroism as a fight for “who we are as a people”.
The prime minister joined hundreds of veterans, family members and dignitaries at a commemoration of the start of the campaign in Canberra on Sunday, with nation’s most decorated living soldier and accused war criminal Ben Roberts-Smith among the crowd at the Australian War Memorial.
“In New York, fires were still burning at Ground Zero from the September 11 attacks a month earlier. The world felt upended,” Albanese said of the start of Operation Slipper.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Though it would change so devastatingly a year later in Bali, it was not yet directly our fight.
“Yet Australia did what is so resolutely in our nature. We went to support our friend and ally.
“We went because we saw what was at stake, and we went on the principle that September 11 was an attack on a way of life that belonged just as much to us.”
He said the more than 35,000 defence force members deployed over the following two decades did so because the very freedoms “that are at the heart of who we are as a people and a nation were under threat”.
Roberts-Smith, who denies the allegations against him, attended the event alongside family members and supporters, as well as former prime ministers John Howard, Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison.
The governor general, Sam Mostyn, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, were also present in the bright sunshine.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson tells rally Ben Roberts-Smith is a person ‘I respect and I admire’
Roberts-Smith was awarded Australia’s highest military honour – the Victoria Cross – for his service in Afghanistan, but now faces accusations he murdered five unarmed detainees during his deployment.
The former Special Air Service regiment corporal sat alongside his partner, Sarah Matulin, after a judge agreed to vary his bail conditions to allow him to visit Canberra .
Deployments to the Middle East continued until withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021.
US troops left a few months later after signing an agreement with the Taliban, who swiftly returned to power and reintroduced authoritarian control, including strict suppression of women and girls’ rights.
Some 47 Australian personnel died as a result of their service and 263 were wounded, while thousands more allied soldiers were killed.
Tens of thousands of civilians were also estimated to have been killed during the war.
Despite the controversy over Australia’s military involvement in Afghanistan and its legacy, the troops who served on the ground remain intensely proud of what they achieved.
Soldier Mathew Bell was deployed in 2012, aged 24, with his infantry battalion to a forward operating base in Afghanistan’s “badlands” west of Tarinkot.
More than a decade after he returned to Australia, Bell remembers his unit’s work with a sense of honour and accomplishment.
“We changed that little part of Afghanistan, that little part of the world for good,” the former lance corporal, now 38, said.
Bell said girls were able to attend school, medical services were rolled out to villages and “there was freedom”.
“Not the oppression we’re seeing now under the Taliban government,” the father of two said.
“Our role was essentially to go out on either vehicle-mounted patrols or foot patrols, out among the local population through the desert, through the green zone, keeping the Taliban at bay.
“It was a hot area. Once you stepped over that line in the sand, like, that was Taliban territory.”
One of Bell’s close mates was badly wounded in a roadside bomb explosion and on more than one occasion, his section was pinned down by sniper fire.
Services were also held at the Anzac Memorial in Sydney’s Hyde Park, at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance and other sites around the country.
Australians who served in the Afghanistan War were deployed in various roles and missions contributing to reconstruction efforts, democratic governance, training and humanitarian aid.
Operation Slipper was followed between 2015 and 2021 by Operation Highroad and the Kabul airlift in August 2021.

‘Under tremendous strain’: CIA analyst turned spy novelist on a fraying US-UK alliance
David McCloskey’s new book depicts a calamitous collapse of the ‘special relationship’ – could things get darker still?
The “special relationship”, the time-honored emotional bond between the US and Britain that has sustained through war and peace, is in trouble.
The ties of history, culture and language that have bridged an ocean and bound the two countries politically for generations are fraying as perhaps never before – strained relentlessly by Donald Trump , who has gleefully sacrificed traditional alliances and diplomatic niceties on the altar of his “America first” agenda.
US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
Against that troubled backdrop, David McCloskey, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analyst turned spy writer and podcast host, has sketched out how things could get darker still. His case – laid out in a new novel – has been reinforced by the serendipity of real events.
The past month alone has seen the US president openly consider abandoning Washington’s de facto support for Britain in its dispute with Argentina over the Falklands Islands, and vocally welcome the idea of a united Ireland.
Last weekend, the Trump administration hurriedly withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from a British airbase, RAF Fairford, following intelligence reports that they could be targeted in an Iranian drone attack. The move, presaged by jeering attacks on Britain from some of Trump’s most ardent supporters, reinforced a growing sense of the US pulling back from a strategic partnership that, at times, has been intimate.
Nothing denotes the special in the relationship between the US and Britain as the sharing of intelligence. In London Station, his new novel, McCloskey somewhat ghoulishly explores where it could all go wrong, depicting a calamitous collapse in cooperation as the CIA comes under the guidance of a new Trump-like director who scorns MI6, the British intelligence agency, as “freeloaders” and “pickpockets”.
McCloskey’s imagined scenario seemed plausible even before recent developments, as two allies that faced the cold war and other conflicts in lockstep drifted apart on a number of fronts, including Russia’s war with Ukraine and Trump’s decision to attack Iran, signaling a geopolitical trend that he calls “fairly alarming”.
“I do think we’re at a period in the special relationship where there’s a lot more divergence between [Britain and the US],” said McCloskey, speaking by phone from a London cab. “A lot of the cultural affinity that the two nations have have felt for each other, going back to the second world war, is thinning out a little bit – and it created a lot of opportunities to think about how this relationship, as shown in the novel, could get even worse.”
The “ton of research” McCloskey carried out while writing uncovered serious fears for the special relationship’s future on both sides, but especially in Britain. “We’re seeing a lot of concern here in London about what do we do with this really hard-elbowed US foreign policy under Trump that seems to minimize the contribution of of allies and sort of pull traditional enemies closer,” he said. “So I think I think the relationship is under a tremendous amount of strain.”
One source of British concern is Trump’s affinity for Vladimir Putin, which has left British spies leery of sharing information for fear that the US president could pass it on, or betray the source.
“If I was deep inside Vauxhall Cross [the London headquarters of MI6] working on Russia, and I had a very sensitive piece of intelligence from a sensitive source, would I have more qualms about sharing that with the Americans right now? Probably,” suggested McCloskey, recalling the occasion when Trump reportedly passed on Israeli intelligence to the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, during his first presidency.
Worried British intelligence officers McCloskey has consulted had posited such a scenario “as a reasonable hypothetical”, he said, quickly adding that he could not confirm if any intelligence had actually been withheld.
What he could verify was tension, resentment on the British side at being the junior partner, and – curiously – mutual feelings of intimidation, with US agents being deferential to the UK side’s native abilities.
“One of the very common themes of my conversations with UK intelligence officers was this feeling of real tension with the US and fear because there wasn’t anything the UK, as the junior partner, could really do about it,” said McCloskey, who regularly unpicks murky realities of the British-US intelligence partnership with the former BBC security correspondent Gordon Corera on The Rest Is Classified podcast.
“For example, if you’re in a third country and you have an [MI6] officer and a CIA officer pursuing the same target, and both services sort of deconflict that, it was almost always the case that the US would win out because it just has more heft and more resources,” he said. “Many of the MI6 [insiders] I interviewed, I think, frankly, resented the [CIA] and didn’t care for it. Yet there was this sense of like, ‘What can I do? We’re very reliant on this partner.’”
CIA officers had their own problems. “I found any number of CIA officers who could recount instances where they had personality conflicts with their British counterparts,” said McCloskey. “The CIA officers felt here was a intimidation [from] the Brits, stemming from education, how articulate they were, their sense of refinement.”
US agents, virtually without exception, saw merit in the alliance. “Almost every CIA officer I spoke to really felt like the Brits brought a great deal to the table,” recounted McCloskey.
The “five-eyes” cooperation agreement – providing signals intelligence-sharing between the US, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand – remains intact, and is likely to survive for the foreseeable future.
The US-UK relationship still has “depth and flexibility”, in McCloskey’s view, giving it the potential to evolve and survive, regardless of future leadership in either country.
Nevertheless, he conceded, things have permanently changed. Tensions between the intelligence services will likely escalate – albeit not necessarily to the extent depicted in London Station – as foreign policy interests of the US and UK go their separate ways.
“A lot of the structural changes we’re seeing in the special relationship are not specific to Trump, and will outlast him,” McCloskey said. “Unlike the cold war, we don’t have an overarching geopolitical enemy to unify us, and so we’re seeing more divergence.
“There’s are a lot of areas where I could imagine the two intelligence services slightly downshifting their level of exchange.”
The end result is a relationship that may remain friendly, at times close – but perhaps less than special.
“Framing it as a special relationship makes it seem like the two countries should agree on almost everything at all times, everywhere – and that is too much pressure to put on a bilateral relationship between two independent nations,” concluded McCloskey. “It’s a cliche, but true, that nations don’t have permanent relationships – just interests.”

items.title: Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
items.summary: Medical services in Taiz risk shutting down as fuel, medicines, and supplies run alarmingly low under Houthi blockade.
items.content:
Share Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government on social media
People shop at a market in Yemen's southwestern city of Taiz on October 8, 2026 [AFP]
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has warned of an “imminent health and humanitarian catastrophe” in the besieged city of Taiz, in the country’s southwest, as the Houthis continue their siege and “obstruct essential supplies”.
Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said in a statement on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.

It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”.
Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said.
It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid.
It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities.
“Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said.
The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast.
Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre.
The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed.
The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.
Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October.
Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.
He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced.
Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58).
“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.
The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organization have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril.
“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization.

items.title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
items.summary: Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".
items.content:
Image caption, The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday
Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".
The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.
"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.
However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.
It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.
Figure caption, Watch: Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay?
Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.
Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure MarÃ­a Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.
Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".
He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

Sun 11 Oct 2026 06.36 EDT First published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 04.23 EDT
Global condemnation of 'attack on civilians'

This image from video obtained and verified by AP shows thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh Photograph: AP
This image from video obtained and verified by AP shows thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh Photograph: AP
The Houthis this morning have just also issued a warning to travellers and airlines to stay away from Saudi airports following yesterday’s attack.
It’s the first public message from the group since Saturday’s deadly assault.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Mecca and Medina – the holiest cities in Islam - were excepted but the other Saudi airports and airspace “are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces”.
He warned the public to “take our warning seriously” and also claimed that “Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions”.
The Gulf state has been asking the US and other Western allies for more missile interceptors since the fighting escalated.
Sahree ended his post by saying his group is pursuing: “airport for airport, siege for siege, and escalation for escalation” until they achieved their goals.
All week the Houthis have been striking the main airport in the Saudi capital as Saudi Arabia has increased strikes on Houthi territory in Yemen. The Houthi-run health ministry says 91 Yemenis have been killed and 168 injured in the past five weeks due to Saudi-led attacks. It said 60% of those killed were women and children.
This week, the Saudi-led coalition backing the Yemeni government forces launched a major counter-offensive to try and push back the rebel group who’ve rapidly seized and gained territory since September.
The Houthis have taken over islands in the Bab al- Mandab strait and also staked positions along the Red Sea, tightening their grip on the crucial passageway through which Saudi Arabia, a top oil exporter, had been diverting flows as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut off.
Global condemnation of 'attack on civilians'
12 killed at Riyadh airport and hundreds wounded in Saturday strike
Why else has the US been reluctant to intervene so far in Saudi Arabia’s fight?
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
Saturday’s attack might change things but Donald Trump has been reluctant so far to help out Saudi Arabia for several reasons, as my colleague Patrick Wintour explains:
The US has its hands full and its munitions stocks are empty due to the war in Iran.
Ahead of the midterms, Donald Trump does not want to launch another forever war.
After bombing the Houthis for 50 days in spring 2025, he struck a bilateral ceasefire with the Houthis – a deal that excluded Israel.
He has twice rejected Saudi pleas that the fate of the strait is a matter for the world.
Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
An American citizen was among the 12 killed in the airport attack yesterday. For weeks now there’s been speculation over whether the US will join Saudi Arabia in carrying out air strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
When fighting recommenced last month with the Houthis , Saudi Crown ​Prince Mohammed bin Salman had reportedly called Donald Trump to request military assistance. The US president committed only military intelligence and targeting help rather than send war planes.
On Saturday, following the deadly airport attack, Trump was asked by reporters if the US would take a more active position and join in the Saudi strikes.
“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.
He later said he also planned to speak with Saudi Arabia’s leader.
Asked again by reporters if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, “We’ll find out.”
The fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen this past month have marked a new front in the Iran war, further driving up global oil and fuel prices as Saudi Arabia is the world’s top oil exporter and had been delivering its output through the Red Sea which has seen shipping attacks by Iran’s ally in recent weeks.
The US is now in the seventh month of the war it began against Iran in February, and across American states gasoline prices have surged 47%.
Trump’s approval rating has also dropped from 41% in Feburary to 37%- his lowest level yet ahead of the midterm elections next month.
There’s been a strong condemnation of this morning of the Houthi’s deadly strike on Saudi Arabia’s largest airport. Global leaders say attacks on civilians must stop.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply shocked” by Saturday’s strike.
“Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately,” he said.
Meanwhile EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union stands “in solidarity with Saudi Arabia”, noting the “murderous attack on civilians” as a “dangerous escalation” in the wider war.
These "attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world,” she said.
The EU as a bloc has not sent any direct military aid to Saudi Arabia since fighting recommenced with the Houthis last month. The Saudis have asked France and Germany directly for aid but the European powers haven’t commited.
The UK meanwhile has sent air defences and RAF Voyager refuelling aircraft to Saudi Arabia since late September, in part says the government to help keep Red Sea oil flows open.
This morning UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Houthi attacks on civilian sites “is one of the reasons why the UK is providing support to Saudi Arabia in the form of air defences and air-to-air resupplying”.
Meanwhile in the Middle East region, Iraq , which neighbours Saudi Arabia, warned this morning that the attack endangered “regional security and stability”.

King Khalid remains closed today. It remains to be seen if operations will continue at other Saudi airports.
The Houthis earlier in the week had warned commercial airlines “for the last time” about the consequences of flying into Saudi airspace, noting it was a theatre of fighting.
Several airlines have previously suspended flights during the past month as the Iran War has expanded to this new front. Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines had all temporarily paused their routes into Riyadh and other Saudi cities.

Saturday’s attack was the third launched on the Saudi capital’s main airport this week- with the missile making it past Saudi air defences to strike terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid airport where hundreds of passengers were awaiting domestic flights.
The attack killed at least 12 people and injured 309 at last count, say Saudi officials.
The dead include four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis .
The Dammam airport has been an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.

All eyes will be on the bellwether of the semiconductor sector.
TSMC’s HPC numbers will reveal the AI market’s strengths and weaknesses.
Its 3nm chip production should account for a bigger slice of its revenue.
The bulls will expect it to raise its revenue guidance again.

TSMC (NYSE: TSM) , the world's top contract chipmaker, will post its full third-quarter earnings report on Oct. 15. It already disclosed that its revenue grew 50% year over year during the quarter, but three yet-to-be-released numbers might drive its stock higher or lower.
Most of TSMC's growth is being driven by its production of high-performance computing (HPC) chips for Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and other fabless AI chipmakers . That segment accounted for two-thirds of its revenue in the second quarter, and its sequential growth accelerated in the first half of the year as the demand for AI chips (especially Nvidia's) outstripped its supply. That growth is consistently offsetting its slower production of other types of chips.
Therefore, investors should keep a close eye on TSMC's HPC revenue growth. Any hint of a slowdown could attract the bears, but a meaningful acceleration might drive its stock higher.
TSMC maintains its lead in the "process race" against Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) and other foundries by producing the world's smallest, densest, and most power-efficient chips.
Over the past year, the weight of its top-tier 3nm chips on its top line has increased, while the weight of its 5nm and 7nm nodes has decreased. The 3nm node includes Nvidia's newest Vera Rubin platform, which entered full production in early 2026. Investors will be expecting TSMC to generate even more revenue from the 3nm node in the second half of 2026.
Last but not least, the bulls will expect TSMC to raise its full-year revenue guidance again. Back in January, TSMC expected its revenue to grow in the mid-to-high 20% range in USD terms. But in its first-quarter report in April, it raised its outlook to more than 30% growth.
During its second-quarter report in July, it raised its guidance again to at least 40% growth. If it doesn't reiterate or raise that outlook -- which seems unlikely since its revenue rose 50% year over year in the third quarter -- its stock could pull back. That could also happen if it merely reiterates its revenue guidance but raises its capex guidance (as it did in the second quarter).
Therefore, TSMC could seemingly hit a home run on Oct. 15, but these three numbers could prevent its stock from rallying. They could also weigh down the broader semiconductor sector -- so investors holding chip stocks must keep a close eye on this earnings report.

items.title: Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an ‘emergency brake’ that humans control
items.summary: Nadella joined other tech moguls and researchers in calling for stronger safeguards and, in some cases, for the pacing of frontier development.
items.content:
Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an ‘emergency brake’ humans control
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said advanced AI systems should include containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake."
Other AI and tech industry leaders have called for stronger safeguards and, in several cases, pacing frontier development.
President Donald Trump opposes slowing U.S. AI development, while his administration has launched a safety-focused task force.
Satya Nadella, chief executive officer of Microsoft Corp., during an event in San Francisco, California, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026.
Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake" that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task.
"We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X.
"Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system," he said.
Nadella's comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates , Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast.
An AI researcher quit Anthropic last month and accused the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of "gambling with our lives." Later that day, an alignment lead at Anthropic focused on AI safety said there's a greater than 10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans" within the next decade.
Conversely, President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed AI extinction risks and has instead emphasized that the industry needs to stay ahead of China. Trump also recently introduced a new "AI Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton , to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors.
Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability."
They include model diversity; a human-readable footprint of the model's actions; continuous system testing; independent controls and auditability; containment; and incident disclosure, Nadella wrote.
"The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most," he wrote. "It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least."

items.title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
items.summary: The White House had blocked access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, leading them to restrict pool coverage.
items.content:
Image caption, The row over the White House pool affected live TV coverage of Trump events last month
The US justice department (DoJ) has said it is investigating several TV networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump.
Last month, five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days in response to the Trump administration withdrawing the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico.
The justice department asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the pool and said that the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, referring to a law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.
Pool members usually share their material with the wider media.
A DoJ spokesperson said: "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ânews organisations have violated the antitrust laws."
Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.
The White House later reinstated their access after a ruling from a judge. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.
The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

items.title: What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
items.summary: Fossil fuels produce 81 percent of global energy. We look at Middle East’s role and what happens when supplies are cut.
items.content:
Share What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts on social media
A major energy conference is going ahead in Riyadh from Sunday despite a Houthi attack on the city’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Saudi ⁠Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said on Sunday that the 25th ⁠World Petroleum Council Energy Congress has begun ‌in Riyadh. The 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial will be held on the sidelines of the conference, called Riyadh Energy Week, which is to run until Thursday.
But Italy, the cohost of the IEF, will join the meeting via videolink. Nigeria, the other cohost, is sending a representative to the event.
The IEF brings together 68 countries that account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supplies and demand. Its members include Saudi Arabia, the United States and Russia. The meeting comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy flows and pushed governments to reassess their energy security.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at where the world’s energy comes from, how much is produced in the Middle East and which countries have strategic reserves to fall back on.
Energy heats our homes, fuels our cars, keeps the lights on and runs the factories that make what we buy. It comes from fossil fuels such as oil, coal and gas as well as nuclear power and renewables.
Despite rapid growth in renewables, fossil fuels still account for nearly 81 percent of global energy consumption. Oil is the largest source at 31.4 percent, followed by coal at 25.9 percent and natural gas at 23.5 percent. Traditional biomass, nuclear power and other sources make up the rest.
(Al Jazeera) Production is concentrated in a handful of regions, so disruptions in any of them ripple through global markets.
The Middle East is the largest oil-producing region, and North America is the largest natural gas producer. Russia and Central Asia are also major producers of both.
The Middle East’s importance to energy markets is also about geography. Three narrow waterways connect its producers with consumers around the world.
Before the Iran war, about 27 percent of global seaborne oil trade and almost 20 percent of liquefied natural gas trade transited through the Strait of Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula.
On the peninsula’s western side, the Bab al-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. As the Iran war has spilled over into other areas of the Middle East and Yemen’s civil war has ramped up, traffic has been reduced through both the strait and canal, forcing some energy shipments on longer routes around Africa.
(Al Jazeera) “That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a chokepoint,” said Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service.
He told Al Jazeera that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Gulf ports are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
Further down the supply chain, people and businesses are feeling the disruption through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries that rely on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf face higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find other suppliers. Even where deals have kept goods moving, the extra costs are being passed down the chain.
Eritrea and Madagascar are the most dependent on Middle Eastern oil, each sourcing about 90 percent of their supply from the region. They are followed by Pakistan (78 percent), Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Gas has been even harder to replace than oil because most of it travels as liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz.
Countries that depend on these shipments are paying more for fuel and electricity and competing for a smaller pool of cargoes. Poorer importers with little storage have struggled the most to find alternatives.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern gas are mostly in Asia. South Korea sources 31 percent of the gas it uses from the region, followed by India (29 percent), Pakistan (27 percent) and Taiwan (26 percent).
Countries keep emergency oil stocks for when supplies are cut off or reduced, and these have been the world’s main cushion during the war. That cushion is now wearing thin.
Western countries have little left to release, energy industry leaders warned, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1982.
“Estimates suggest less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today with the vast majority not practically available,” Amin Nasser, head of Saudi Aramco, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
The International Energy Agency, which coordinates emergency stocks for its members, released a record 400 million barrels of oil in March. It is now preparing to release another 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to ease soaring diesel prices although some of this may be oil from the March release that has yet to reach the market.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks in Saudi Arabia are now threatening supplies again, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Before this year’s releases, China held by far the largest reserves, an estimated 1.4 billion barrels, more than the rest of the list combined. The US was second with 413 million barrels, followed by Japan with 263 million.

Saudi Arabia has accused Yemen’s Houthis of killing at least 12 people and wounding 300 others in a third attack on the Riyadh international airport this week.
The victims of the attack on Saturday included four Saudis, two ⁠Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said.
It was the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.
The Riyadh airport attack came as the war in Yemen intensifies, with the Houthis battling forces aligned with the internationally recognised government for control of the country. Saudi Arabia is waging an air campaign against the Houthis to support the ground war by Yemeni government forces against the Iran-backed group.
US President Donald Trump described the attack as “terrible” and said he “will be speaking” with Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), soon. He said he was evaluating whether the US should join the war against the Houthis.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We’ll move very quickly,” he said.

“We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families,” he wrote on X.

House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
Some Republican lawmakers are pushing back on President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia amid rising fuel prices.
WASHINGTON -- Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking Russian oil purchases, challenging President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as lawmakers warn the move could help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.
Fitzpatrick (Republican-Pennsylvania), co-chair of the House Ukraine Caucus, announced on October 10 that he would introduce the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.
“We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick wrote on X. “It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly.”
Representative Don Bacon (Republican-Nebraska) has agreed to co-sponsor the bill. A Democratic sponsor had not been identified.
Trump Says Ukraine Should 'Get A New President' As Russia Kills At Least 20 In Air Strikes
A discharge petition can force a House vote without approval from the relevant committee or House leadership if it secures 218 signatures.
The effort faces time constraints: Congress is not scheduled to resume voting for several weeks, and the current congressional term ends in January. Any bill would also need Senate approval and could face White House opposition.
Fitzpatrick invoked former President Ronald Reagan's approach to confronting Moscow and reaffirmed congressional support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has again criticized.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine. Russia is squarely to blame,” Fitzpatrick wrote, adding that Congress and the American people stood behind Zelenskyy “until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
The proposed legislation reflects concern among some Republicans that easing Russian energy restrictions could undermine pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Representative Michael McCaul (Republican-Texas), the former chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that lifting sanctions could “fund the Kremlin's war machine -- emboldening more violence and destruction.”
He cited the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The law authorizes the president, under specified conditions, to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian energy. McCaul said it gave Trump leverage over Russia and China to help secure a negotiated end to the war.
Senator Lisa Murkowski (Republican-Alaska) urged Trump to use those authorities instead of allowing Russia to earn more from diesel exports.
Exclusive: A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine
“We can discuss Russia's return to global energy markets once the war is over, but in the meantime, we need to cut off everything fueling it,” she wrote on social media.
Democrats and former officials have also pointed to the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has met specified conditions, including withdrawing from Ukraine, recognizing Ukrainian sovereignty and posing no threat to NATO.
The law passed the Senate 100-0 and the House 413-9 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Former Representative Tom Malinowski, also a former top State Department official, urged Democratic leaders to use the law's expedited procedures to challenge the administration's decision.
“Under this law, House and Senate Democratic leaders can introduce a ‘Joint Resolution of Disapproval’ to prevent the purchase of Russian oil, which Congress then has to vote on in an expedited manner,” Malinowski wrote on social media.
Massive Russian Attack Kills At Least 22, Devastates Pryluky Apartment Block
“Schumer and Jeffries should do so ASAP,” he added, referring to Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Whether the 2022 law applies to the latest arrangement remains a key question as the administration's temporary authorization for Russian diesel exports faces scrutiny.
Daniel Balson, advocacy director at Razom for Ukraine, told RFE/RL that Trump's decision undermined the purpose of the sanctions legislation passed weeks earlier.
“Three weeks ago, Congress passed the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. This bill was designed to force other countries to lower their Russian energy dependence. President Trump's recent decision just increased our own,” Balson said.
He urged lawmakers to challenge the move to protect Ukraine and the credibility of congressional action. Although he had not seen Fitzpatrick's bill, Balson said pro-Ukraine advocates would pursue “any and all legislative avenues” to oppose the decision.
Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine who generally votes with Democrats, said in a statement that the agreement would offer little relief to American consumers while benefiting Russia.
Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders
Citing administration figures, King said the deal covered 300,000 tons of diesel for October and 500,000 tons for November -- roughly equivalent to a day's diesel consumption in the United States.
“This so-called deal with Russia will do little for America and much for Vladimir Putin as he seeks to sustain his murderous campaign on Ukraine,” King said. He called the agreement “a fraud.”
Trump on October 10 renewed his attacks on Zelenskyy, saying Ukraine should hold an election and replace its president with a leader willing to reach an agreement with Russia.
“Well, I think he should have an election. And he could have settled this thing many times,” Trump told reporters.
Earlier, Trump had said Ukraine should “get a new leader who can make a deal.” He also demanded that Kyiv “damn well stop” attacking Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine has targeted to disrupt Moscow's war economy and fuel supplies.
Trump blamed Zelenskyy for failing to secure a settlement, a claim at odds with Kyiv’s position that any agreement must protect Ukraine’s sovereignty and with lawmakers’ calls to maintain pressure on Moscow. Trump also portrayed Putin as eager for peace and praised the release of Russian oil onto global markets.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia's war economy is terrible,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
Trump Makes Deal With Putin On Diesel Exports. Ukraine Calls It A 'Gift'
Trump's remarks came hours after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhya.
Zelenskyy has said elections cannot be held under martial law and amid the security risks created by Russia's invasion. Ukrainian officials have also cited the need to ensure soldiers and displaced citizens can participate in a credible vote.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha issued a statement late on October 10 backing the Ukrainian president.
Zelenskyy "leads our nation in a time of war -- a war for independence, freedom, and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support," Sybiha wrote on X.
European officials criticized the diesel agreement, warning that additional Russian energy revenue could help sustain the war.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russian strikes had killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians over the past two days and that Moscow had intensified hybrid attacks against EU member states and NATO allies.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't,” Kallas said, adding that EU foreign ministers planned to announce a major new round of sanctions on October 12 targeting people and organizations supporting Moscow's war effort.
Germany also reaffirmed its commitment to existing sanctions and said it would work with European partners on further measures.
A spokesman for Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Berlin stood by its restrictions, while government spokesman Stefan Kornelius reiterated support for Ukraine. Economics Minister Katherina Reiche also backed the EU sanctions packages.
Germany's Fuels and Energy Trade Association said it did not expect the agreement to have a major effect on petrol-station prices.
House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
Alex Raufoglu is RFE/RL's senior correspondent in Washington, D.C.

Candidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
Leftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of Andes
A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to local election data.
The 45-year-old, who shares two of his names with the notorious European dictators, won the race for mayor of Queropalca, in Peru’s central Huánuco region, and will take office on 1 January.
The candidate from the leftwing Ahora Nación party won 229 out of a total of 663 votes in elections on 4 October, according to the national office of electoral processes.
His closest rival, the far-right candidate Gaspar Osorio, received 204 votes.
Flores, who works in freight transportation, had belonged to Popular Force, the party of Peru’s rightwing president, Keiko Fujimori, until 2025, according to electoral authorities.
Despite the name being associated with Germany’s Nazi leader Adolf Hitler, several candidates with the name have won elections in Peru.
In 2021, the doctor Hitler Saavedra Casternoque was elected to parliament for the centrist party Somos Peru.
In 2018, Hitler Alba Sánchez was voted in as mayor of the Andean district of Yungar, saying during his campaign that he was “the good Hitler”.

‘It was a terrible thing’: Panama declares state of emergency as quake aftershocks rattle communities
More than 100 aftershocks as high as magnitude-5.8 recorded after two quakes toppled buildings and prompted evacuations
Panama’s government has declared a state of emergency on Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours.
Officials did not attribute any deaths to Friday’s 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes, but reported damages in all 10 of Panama’s provinces and two Indigenous territories.
The earthquakes toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.
The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centred about 10km (6 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the US Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10km (6 miles).
A car sits crushed beneath debris from a collapsed building in Penonome, Panama. Photograph: Enea Lebrun/Reuters The presidential minister, Juan Carlos Orillac, announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, the deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, said 27 people had been reported with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.
Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes Panama and triggers panic in capital
About 420 homes and the same number of public schools had been damaged, according to the Civil Protection agency. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.
In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64km (40 miles) north-east of the epicentre, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government’s guidance on what to do next.
“We’ve been here since 1 pm yesterday; we haven’t moved,” Tony Jiménez, whose home partially collapsed, said, while sitting with relatives under a tent. “It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense – truly intense.”
Elodia Oliva (94) rests in a park in downtown Tonosi, Panama, on Saturday. Photograph: Bienvenido Velasco/EPA Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.
That the country appeared to have avoided widespread deaths could be due to its strict building codes, especially governing the construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, the head of the seismology department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Messages of support and offers of assistance were sent from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.
The US Department of State on Saturday said it mobilised a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments. The US government also pledged $5m for humanitarian assistance.
The US military’s southern command said two helicopters, supported by the state department’s drug-control bureau, had delivered 2,000 pounds (907kg) of food to people affected by the earthquakes.
